precepts.text: Haman the Agagite sought to molest Mordecai and his people because of the two eunuchs, the assassins he hired to take the Persian throne from inside.
precepts.point: Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite: Agag was the Amalekite king of 1 Samuel 15, so Haman descended from the Edomites Saul failed to finish, and when he learned Mordecai was of Saul's line he sought to kill them all. From the womb to the tomb, this is war.

note.label: Edom: The Robbers of thy people revealed past and present

precepts.why:
“After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite”. Ahasuerus is Artaxerxes. Haman was the enemy in the book of Esther, the one who sought to kill all the Jews out of existence. And he is called the Agagite: in 1 Samuel 15, Agag was the king of the Amalekites, an Edomite king. Haman was a descendant of the survivors when King Saul went in and slaughtered them.

The Apocrypha tells the same man's story: “Howbeit Aman the son of Amadathus the Agagite, who was in great honour with the king, sought to molest Mardocheus and his people because of the two eunuchs of the king.” When you read Esther, Haman hired two assassins to kill the king and take over the throne. The Greeks infiltrated the Persian Empire and tried to conquer it from the inside.

And when Haman found out that Mordecai was of the same line as King Saul, he said, that's Saul's line, kill them all; they tried to kill us off. They were going to go to war with them from generation to generation. We will never get along, from the womb to the tomb. This is war.

precepts.text: Haman, a Macedonian, a stranger from the Persian blood: Philip was the Macedonian, so Edomites and Macedonians are the same people, and Haman was an Edomite.
precepts.point: Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite: Agag was the Amalekite king of 1 Samuel 15, so Haman descended from the Edomites Saul failed to finish, and when he learned Mordecai was of Saul's line he sought to kill them all. From the womb to the tomb, this is war.

note.label: Edom: The Robbers of thy people revealed past and present

precepts.why:
Esther 3:1 calls Haman the Agagite. Chapter 16 tells you what he was: “For Aman, a Macedonian, the son of Amadatha, being indeed a stranger from the Persian blood”. Haman was a Macedonian.

Now read 1 Maccabees 1:1: “Alexander son of Philip, the Macedonian”. Alexander the Great's father was Philip the Macedonian, who came out of the land of Chettiim and whose son smote Darius king of the Persians and Medes and reigned in his stead, the first over Greece. That is when the Greeks began to conquer the dark nations.

So Haman was called a Macedonian, and Philip was called the Macedonian: Edomites and Macedonians are the same people. Haman was not a Persian; he was “a stranger from the Persian blood”. He was an Edomite, the Agagite, a descendant of Amalek, the enemy of Jacob from generation to generation.

note.label: Esther 3: Haman the Agagite and the Decree to Destroy the Jews

precepts.why:
Haman is “the son of Hammedatha the Agagite”, and that name reaches back to Saul. Saul told Samuel, “Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites.” He had been commanded to utterly destroy them, and he says he did, but he brought Agag the king of Amalek back alive. He spared him.

Because Saul spared Agag, the Agagite line lived on, and Haman is of it: he descends from Amalek. That explains his deep disdain for Israel. When the king set his seat above all the princes and commanded that all bow, an Amalekite was set over the king's gate, and Mordecai the Jew bowed not.

precepts.text: Mordecai's own prayer shows he refused to bow not from contempt but so as not to set the glory of man above the glory of the Most High.
precepts.point: The servants asked daily why Mordecai transgressed the king's commandment, and he hearkened not, but told them he was a Jew, and they told Haman to see whether Mordecai's matter would stand. We do not bow, the same as the three Hebrew children did not bow to the image in Babylon, for we pledge allegiance to none but the Most High.

note.label: Esther 3: Haman the Agagite and the Decree to Destroy the Jews

precepts.why:
“Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence.” The servants asked him daily why he transgressed the king's commandment, and he told them he was a Jew. His own prayer in the Apocrypha gives the reason from the inside: “thou knowest, Lord, that it was neither in contempt nor pride, nor for any desire of glory, that I did not bow down to proud Aman. For I could have been content with good will for the salvation of Israel to kiss the soles of his feet. But I did this, that I might not prefer the glory of man above the glory of God: neither will I worship any but thee, O God, neither will I do it in pride.”

It was not contempt and it was not pride. He would have kissed the soles of Aman's feet for the salvation of Israel. He refused so as not to set the glory of man above the glory of the Most High, and because he would worship none but the Most High.

That is why we do not bow. The three Hebrew children did not bow to the image in Babylon, Mordecai did not bow to Haman, and we pledge allegiance to none but the Most High.

precepts.text: The canonical book promotes the same Aman, the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, setting his seat above all the princes.
precepts.point: The teaching traces who Aman was. He is the same Aman promoted in the canonical book, an Agagite, and the Agagites descend from Agag king of the Amalekites, and Amalek descends from Esau. This is the lineage that has warred against Israel throughout history and has always been unsuccessful, for the Most High delivered his people.

note.label: Esther 12: Mardocheus Uncovers the Plot and Aman's Hatred

precepts.why:
“Aman the son of Amadathus the Agagite, who was in great honour with the king, sought to molest Mardocheus and his people because of the two eunuchs of the king.” When Mardocheus told on the eunuchs and had them put to death, Aman was upset, and he set himself to destroy not Mardocheus only but all the Israelites.

The canonical book shows where that great honour came from: “After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him.” Amadathus is Hammedatha; it is the same Aman, the same Agagite, raised to the seat above all the princes.

Tracing him is the point. An Agagite descends from Agag king of the Amalekites, and Amalek descends from Esau. That is the lineage that has warred against Israel throughout history, and it has always been unsuccessful, for the Most High delivered his people.

precepts.text: Haman was full of wrath because Mardocheus bowed not, and he sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom, not Mardocheus alone.
precepts.point: This sounds exactly like the curses laid out for our people in Deuteronomy 28, where the enemy shows no favor toward the young or the old. Both the ancient and the present generation were marked for the grave in one day.

note.label: Esther 13: The Decree of Destruction and the Prayer of Mardocheus

precepts.why:
The letter goes out in the king's name, but the picture in it is Haman's. The canonical book shows where it began: “when Haman saw that Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence, then was Haman full of wrath.” He “thought scorn to lay hands on Mordecai alone; for they had shewed him the people of Mordecai: wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus, even the people of Mordecai.”

One man would not bow, and Haman's wrath went out to a whole nation. That is why the letter is not about Mardocheus; it is about “a certain malicious people” scattered “in all nations throughout the world”, and why it commands that they “all, with their wives and children, be utterly destroyed by the sword of their enemies, without all mercy and pity”. The order is for the destruction of the Israelites, young and old together, because Haman scorned to lay hands on one alone.

precepts.text: Haman told the king of a people scattered abroad whose laws are diverse, offered ten thousand talents of silver, and the king gave him his ring to seal the decree.
precepts.point: This sounds exactly like the curses laid out for our people in Deuteronomy 28, where the enemy shows no favor toward the young or the old. Both the ancient and the present generation were marked for the grave in one day.

note.label: Esther 13: The Decree of Destruction and the Prayer of Mardocheus

precepts.why:
The slander in the letter is what Haman told the king. “There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the people in all the provinces of thy kingdom; and their laws are diverse from all people; neither keep they the king’s laws: therefore it is not for the king’s profit to suffer them.” The letter repeats it: a people “scattered”, with “laws contrary to all nations”, that “continually despised the commandments of kings”, and “this people alone is continually in opposition unto all men, differing in the strange manner of their laws”. Haman painted Israel as a mischievous, malicious nation so the uniting of the kingdoms could not go forward, and the letter carries his painting.

Then he bought it: “let it be written that they may be destroyed: and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver to the hands of those that have the charge of the business, to bring it into the king’s treasuries.” “And the king took his ring from his hand, and gave it unto Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the Jews’ enemy.” That ring sealed the letter. That is why the ones to be destroyed are they that are “signified in writing unto you by Aman, who is ordained over the affairs, and is next unto us”: the Jews' enemy held the king's ring and wrote the decree.
